conclusion.justification: The report finds that there is 'some evidence' from an encouraging randomized controlled trial showing symptom reduction, but notes that the overall evidence base is thin and the claim is not strongly established. This cautiously favorable stance corresponds to leans_endorse.

report:
**Conclusion:** There is *some* evidence that acupuncture tailored for depression can reduce depressive symptoms during pregnancy, but the claim is not yet strongly established. The key evidence is one relatively small randomized controlled trial of 150 pregnant women with major depressive disorder. It compared depression-specific acupuncture with nonspecific (“control”) acupuncture and massage; the study reported symptom reduction and a higher response rate for depression-specific acupuncture than the control groups.  
https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/fulltext/2010/03000/acupuncture_for_depression_during_pregnancy__a.7.aspx

This is encouraging because it used random allocation and active comparison groups, rather than simply measuring change before and after acupuncture. However, it was short-term, and its result alone cannot show that acupuncture is as effective as established depression treatments, prevents relapse, or improves maternal/infant outcomes.

The broader evidence base appears thin: a systematic review of acupuncture for major depressive disorder found that only one of five studies measuring response found a significantly higher response rate for depression-specific versus nonspecific acupuncture—and that study was the pregnancy trial above.  
https://www.rand.org/content/dam/rand/pubs/research_reports/RR1100/RR1135/RAND_RR1135.pdf

Safety evidence in pregnancy is also limited for detecting rare harms. A pregnancy-focused systematic review noted a twin premature delivery and neonatal death in the Manber trial, judged unrelated to acupuncture by the investigators and safety board; that does not establish causation, but illustrates why larger safety studies matter.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4112450/

For care decisions, don’t substitute acupuncture for assessment and evidence-based depression treatment. ACOG has a dedicated guideline on treatment/management of mental-health conditions in pregnancy and postpartum.  
https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/clinical-practice-guideline/articles/2023/06/treatment-and-management-of-mental-health-conditions-during-pregnancy-and-postpartum
